notes:
Here are the verse-by-verse notes on 2 Chronicles 34, drawn from the sources I was able to access:

---

## 2 Chronicles 34 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary

### v. 1 — Josiah's Age and Reign

Josiah became king at only eight years old after the assassination of his father Amon. His reign of 31 years (640–609 BC) spanned a critical period when Assyrian power collapsed and Babylon rose. Because of his youth, the early years were likely guided by counselors and priests. The name "Josiah" means "Yahweh supports/heals/upholds," a fitting description of his mission to restore true worship and repair the temple. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-34/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-34/) ; [https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-34-commentary](https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-34-commentary)

Matthew Henry notes that, like Joash and Manasseh before him, Josiah was a child-king; though his infancy did not bar him from his right to rule, the early years probably saw others managing affairs, so reformation did not begin immediately. [https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-34-commentary](https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-34-commentary)

A remarkable detail: an unnamed prophet from Judah had predicted Josiah by name roughly 300 years before his birth (1 Kings 13:2). EnduringWord calls this the fulfillment of "the prophecy of 'the man of God out of Judah.'" [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-34/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-34/)

### v. 2 — Josiah's Character Summary

Josiah "did what was right in the sight of the LORD," walked in David's ways, and "did not turn aside to the right or to the left." PreceptAustin notes this is a threefold description: do right, walk right, walk straight. The phrase "did not turn aside" is not used of any other king of Judah, marking Josiah uniquely. He is a living illustration of 2 Chronicles 16:9 — "the eyes of the LORD move to and fro throughout the earth that He may strongly support those whose heart is completely His." [https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-34-commentary](https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-34-commentary)

Guzik adds that this is a general description of his reign, not specifically what he was like at age eight. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-34/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-34/)

### v. 3 — Josiah Seeks God; Begins Reform

In his 8th regnal year (age 16), Josiah "began to seek the God of his father David." In his 12th year (age 20), he began purging idolatry. Guzik notes that "seeking" in Chronicles describes the habit of looking to God in every situation (cf. 2 Chron. 7:14; 30:19). PreceptAustin's chronology stresses that Josiah began reforms *before* he ever heard the Book of the Law read — his seeking of God preceded his encounter with Scripture. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-34/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-34/) ; [https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-34-commentary](https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-34-commentary)

Gill adds that Josiah was in his sixteenth year of age, and cites Kimchi who thought it was the very year his reign began; Jarchi notes it may mean "though he was young, he began to seek after the God of David." The Targum renders it "to seek instruction or doctrine of the Lord God of David his father." [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_chronicles/34.htm](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_chronicles/34.htm)

Matthew Henry: "It is the duty and interest of young people…as soon as they come to years of understanding, to begin to seek God; for those that seek him early shall find him." [https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-34-commentary](https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-34-commentary)

Payne (cited by Guzik) connects the timing to the Scythian invasions (628–626 BC) that "wrought terror among complacent Jews" (cf. Jer. 6:22-24; Zeph. 1:12). [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-34/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-34/)

**Denominational note — Reformed (Ligonier):** Emphasizes that Josiah's faithfulness *predated* the rediscovery of the Law. The author of 2 Kings places the cleansing *after* the book's discovery for theological reasons — to stress that, for an exiled audience, "the only way forward was through a rediscovery of God's law that led to reform." [https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/josiahs-covenant-faithfulness](https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/josiahs-covenant-faithfulness)

### v. 4 — Destruction of Idols

The altars of the Baals were torn down "in his presence" — Josiah personally oversaw the destruction. The "incense altars that were above them" (sun-images, Hebrew *chamanim*) were cut down. Gill explains these sun-images may have been connected to the deity Cham/Ham or Jupiter Ammon, set above the altars facing the sun. [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_chronicles/34.htm](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_chronicles/34.htm)

Guzik emphasizes that the idols were crushed to dust and scattered "over the graves of those who had sacrificed to them" — an act of defilement that showed the utter worthlessness of the idols. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-34/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-34/)

Trapp (cited by Guzik): "Five or six several words are here used, to show how he mawled them, and made mortar of them, as we say; such was his holy indignation, zeal, and revenge." [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-34/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-34/)

### v. 5 — Burning the Priests' Bones

Josiah burned the bones of the idolatrous priests on their own altars. Guzik explains this accomplished two purposes: (1) it carried out the prescribed punishment for idolatrous priests, and (2) it defiled those pagan altars permanently, rendering them unusable. Gill notes this fulfilled the prophecy from 1 Kings 13:2 made over 350 years earlier. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-34/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-34/) ; [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_chronicles/34.htm](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_chronicles/34.htm)

Guzik also stresses that thorough reformation "cannot only deal with sinful things; it must also deal with sinful people. If sinful people are not dealt with, they will quickly bring back the sinful things." [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-34/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-34/)

### vv. 6–7 — Reform Extends into the Former Northern Kingdom

Josiah extended his purging campaign into the territories of Manasseh, Ephraim, Simeon, and "as far as Naphtali" — the northernmost region of the former kingdom of Israel. Gill explains that since the ten tribes had been carried captive by Assyria, those left behind became subject to the kings of Judah. The word translated "ruins" (or "mattocks" in some versions) is understood by Gill as "their desolate places" — areas depopulated by the Assyrian exile. [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_chronicles/34.htm](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_chronicles/34.htm)

Poole (cited by Guzik): "For it must be remembered that the ten tribes were now gone into captivity; and those who were come in their stead were weak and few, and not able to withstand the power of Josiah." [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-34/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-34/)

Constable notes that many Simeonites had allied themselves with Israel religiously (cf. 2 Chron. 15:9). [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-chronicles-34.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-chronicles-34.html)

**Differences in chronology:** The Chronicler places this cleansing before the temple repair and book discovery (12th year), whereas 2 Kings 23 groups all reforms after the 18th-year discovery. Constable explains that the Kings account may have arranged material out of chronological order for theological purposes. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-chronicles-34.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-chronicles-34.html) ; [https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/josiahs-covenant-faithfulness](https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/josiahs-covenant-faithfulness)

### v. 8 — Temple Repair Ordered (18th Year)

In his 18th year (age 26), having purged the land, Josiah turned to repairing the neglected temple. Gill notes it had not been repaired since the time of Joash — about 218 years according to Jewish chronology. The officials sent were Shaphan (scribe), Maaseiah (governor of the city), and Joah (the recorder/remembrancer). [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_chronicles/34.htm](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_chronicles/34.htm)

Guzik notes that Jeremiah, son of this same Hilkiah the high priest, began his prophetic ministry during Josiah's reign (Jer. 1:1-2). Josiah may also have been motivated by remembering King Jehoash's earlier temple restoration (2 Kings 12). [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-34/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-34/)

### vv. 9–11 — Collection and Distribution of Funds

Money was collected by Levite doorkeepers from "Manasseh and Ephraim, from all the remnant of Israel, Judah, and Benjamin." The funds were entrusted to supervisors who paid the workmen and purchased materials — dressed stone, timbers for couplings and beams. The buildings "which the kings of Judah had destroyed" refers to the neglect and abuse under Manasseh and Amon. [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_chronicles/34.htm](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_chronicles/34.htm) ; [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-34/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-34/)

### vv. 12–13 — The Faithful Workmen and Levite Supervisors

"The men did the work faithfully" — Guzik notes Josiah understood the need for organization and funding. The overseers included Jahath and Obadiah (sons of Merari), and Zechariah and Meshullam (sons of Kohath). Gill notes that even Levites "skilled with instruments of music" were assigned to oversee the laborers — "perhaps they might play…on their instruments of music, while the men were at work, that they might go on in it the more pleasantly and cheerfully." [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_chronicles/34.htm](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_chronicles/34.htm) ; [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-34/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-34/)

Other Levites served as secretaries (scribes), officers, and gatekeepers. Guzik summarizes: a well-organized, faithfully executed restoration. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-34/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-34/)

### vv. 14–15 — Discovery of the Book of the Law

While bringing out the money, Hilkiah the priest "found the Book of the Law of the LORD written by Moses." Guzik notes that Deuteronomy 31:24-27 required a copy of this book to be placed beside the ark of the covenant. It had been neglected — Payne (cited by Guzik) says it "become misplaced during the apostate administrations of Manasseh and Amon, under whom the ark had been moved about (2 Chron. 35:3)." [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-34/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-34/)

**What was the book?** Constable states that most scholars believe it was Deuteronomy, citing Dillard for seven supporting reasons, though Payne says it could be part of the Pentateuch or the whole Pentateuch. Clarke (cited by Guzik) thought it might be the very autograph of Moses — specifically Deuteronomy 28–31 containing the covenant renewal and curses. Selman (cited by Guzik) cautions that "neither Kings nor Chronicles provides direct evidence for the thesis…that the scroll was composed as part of a Deuteronomic reform movement." [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-chronicles-34.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-chronicles-34.html) ; [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-34/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-34/)

**How could the Law be lost so quickly?** Constable explains: written copies were scarce; instruction was mostly oral (2 Chron. 17:9); only one generation separated the people from ignorance of God's will (cf. Deut. 6:6-7; 17:18). This "has been true throughout history." [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-chronicles-34.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-chronicles-34.html)

### vv. 16–18 — Shaphan Reports and Reads Before the King

Shaphan first reported on the work progress ("Your servants are doing all that has been placed in their hands…They have paid out the money"), then told the king about the book Hilkiah had given him, and read it aloud in Josiah's presence. Selman (cited by Guzik) notes that "Shaphan confirms that the find took place in the context of the workers' faithfulness." [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-34/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-34/)

Guzik draws the application that throughout church history — including Peter Waldo and the Waldenses — "when the word of God is recovered and spread, then spiritual revival follows." [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-34/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-34/)

### v. 19 — Josiah Tears His Clothes

"When the king heard the words of the Law, he tore his clothes" — a traditional expression of horror and grief. Guzik says this was not "passive information-gathering" but "deep spiritual conviction" and "the kind of conviction of sin that marks true spiritual awakening." He cites Jesus' promise in John 16:8 that the Spirit would convict the world of sin. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-34/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-34/)

Selman (cited by Guzik) quotes a medieval Archbishop of Canterbury who "assumed that Josiah listened to the whole book at one sitting: 'What a contrast to our present-day kings and magnates! If once a year they hear the word of God preached, they find it nauseating and leave the church before the end of the sermon.'" [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-34/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-34/)

### vv. 20–21 — Josiah Sends to Inquire of the LORD

Josiah commissioned a delegation — Hilkiah, Ahikam, Abdon (called Achbor in Kings), Shaphan, and Asaiah — to "inquire of the LORD." His words reveal his grasp of the situation: "Great is the wrath of the LORD that has been poured out on us because our fathers have not kept the word of the LORD by doing all that is written in this book." Guzik notes that Josiah was "so under the conviction of sin that he did not know what to do next." [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-34/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-34/)

### v. 22 — Huldah the Prophetess

The delegation went to Huldah, wife of Shallum, "keeper of the wardrobe," who lived in Jerusalem's Second District. Guzik observes that though prophets Jeremiah and Zephaniah were active at this time, they chose Huldah — "perhaps spiritual, perhaps practical" reasons. Clarke (cited by Guzik) notes: "a pontiff, a pope, a bishop, or a priest, may, in some cases, not possess the true knowledge of God; and…a simple woman, possessing the life of God in her soul, may have more knowledge of the divine testimonies than many of those whose office it is to explain and enforce them." [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-34/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-34/)

### vv. 23–25 — Huldah's Message of Judgment

Huldah's oracle has two parts. First (vv. 23-25): God will bring calamity "according to all the curses written in the book," because the people "have forsaken Me and burned incense to other gods." His wrath "will be poured out upon this place and will not be quenched." Guzik: "Judah and its leaders had acted against the LORD for too long, and would not genuinely repent so as to avoid eventual judgment." Constable adds: "Huldah announced that God had decreed captivity for Judah." [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-34/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-34/) ; [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-chronicles-34.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-chronicles-34.html)

### vv. 26–28 — Huldah's Personal Word for Josiah

Because Josiah's heart was "tender" and he "humbled himself," tore his clothes, and wept, God heard him. The promise: "I will indeed gather you to your fathers, and you will be gathered to your grave in peace. Your eyes will not see all the calamity."

**Baptist (Spurgeon):** In his sermon "Self-Humbling" on this verse, Spurgeon contrasts being *humble* with being *humbled*: "Pharaoh was humbled, but he was not humble." He emphasizes that Josiah's act "was a real and personal act…voluntary…a very deep and thorough one. It was not garment-tearing merely, it was heart-breaking." Spurgeon sees a pastoral reason God sent this discovery: "God had much love towards Josiah, and…knowing the natural tendency of the human heart to pride, He sent him this discovery of the book of the law, to keep him humble at the time when otherwise he might have been exposed to peril." [https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/self-humbling (sermon text in search results)] ; [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-34/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-34/)

**The "died in peace" problem:** Josiah died in battle (2 Chron. 35:20-24). Guzik offers three resolutions: (1) he died before the exile; (2) he was gathered to his fathers who were in peace; (3) he died in God's favor, though by an enemy's hand. Selman: "this does not invalidate God's promise which really means that the exile would not take place during Josiah's lifetime." Constable notes another view: the promise "refers to what would have happened if Josiah had not violated the will of God by engaging Neco in battle." [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-34/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-34/) ; [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-chronicles-34.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-chronicles-34.html)

**G. Campbell Morgan** (cited by Guzik): Josiah's heroism was that "he went on with the work of reformation, even when he knew that nationally it was foredoomed to failure…No pathway of service is more difficult than that of bearing witness to God, in word and in work, in the midst of conditions which are unresponsive." [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-34/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-34/)

**Reformed (D.A. Carson, via PreceptAustin):** "We are afforded a glimpse of what God expects from us if we live in a time of cataclysmic declension: not philosophizing, but self-humbling, transparent repentance, tears, contrition…precisely because God is so slow to anger…he is more eager to suspend and delay the judgment that is the necessary correlative of his holiness than we are to beg him for mercy." [https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-34-commentary](https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-34-commentary)

### vv. 29–30 — Josiah Reads the Law Publicly

Josiah gathered all the elders, priests, Levites, and people "small and great" to the temple and himself read "all the words of the Book of the Covenant." Guzik emphasizes that Josiah "did not respond with indifference or simple contentment that he would not see the judgment in his day. He wanted to get the kingdom right with God." Selman: "It is especially interesting that he regards the written form of God's word as superior to inherited tradition and is willing to pay the cost of correcting his priorities." [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-34/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-34/)

**Differences with 2 Kings:** Ellicott (BibleHub) notes that the Chronicler substitutes "Levites" for "the prophets" (2 Kings 23:2) — "a natural change to make, seeing that the prophetic order had long been extinct in his day." [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_chronicles/34.htm (referenced in search results)]

D.A. Carson: "The picture of the king himself calling together the elders of Judah and solemnly reading to them the Scripture is enormously moving. There is nothing that our generation needs more than to hear the Word of God — and this at a time of biblical illiteracy rising at an astonishing rate." [https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-34-commentary](https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-34-commentary)

### v. 31 — Josiah's Covenant

Josiah "stood by the pillar" (or "in his place") and made a covenant to follow the LORD with all his heart and soul. Guzik notes the Hebrew idiom is literally "'cut a covenant,' which goes back to the practice of cutting the carcass of an animal." [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-34/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-34/)

**Reformed (Ligonier):** "Josiah's zeal for the true worship of the Lord serves as an example for us…Josiah as a model for reformation." The author of 2 Kings wants readers in exile to see that the way forward requires rediscovery of and commitment to God's law. [https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/josiahs-covenant-faithfulness](https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/josiahs-covenant-faithfulness)

### v. 32 — The People Take a Stand

Josiah "had everyone in Jerusalem and Benjamin take a stand in agreement." Guzik says this shows that "God's Spirit extended the work beyond the king to the whole community." It was not mere royal coercion; the people publicly entered the covenant. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-34/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-34/)

### v. 33 — Reforms Completed; Outward Obedience Maintained

Josiah removed "all the abominations" throughout Israel and required everyone to serve the LORD. "Throughout his reign they did not turn aside from following the LORD, the God of their fathers."

Gill offers a crucial qualification: this was not a deep, universal heart-change. There "were great declensions and corruptions among them, as the prophecies of Jeremiah and Zephaniah show." Matthew Henry likewise notes: "Yet despite this sincere revival, the people's hearts were not fully changed, and after his reign, Judah quickly declined, leading to inevitable judgment (2 Kings 23:25–27)." [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_chronicles/34.htm](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_chronicles/34.htm) ; [https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-34-commentary](https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-34-commentary)

---

## Points of Traditional Agreement

Across the sources consulted (EnduringWord/Pentecostal-charismatic, PreceptAustin/evangelical, Ligonier/Reformed, Spurgeon/Baptist, Gill/Baptist, Constable/Dallas Seminary, Matthew Henry/Puritan-Anglican), there is broad agreement on the essential narrative: Josiah's early seeking of God, his zealous reforms, the providential discovery of the Book of the Law, his tender-hearted response, Huldah's dual oracle, and the covenant renewal. All traditions see Josiah as a model of responsiveness to God's Word and true repentance.

## Points of Difference Between Traditions

**Chronology of reforms:** A notable difference between the Chronicler (reforms spread over 8th, 12th, and 18th years) and the author of Kings (all reforms grouped in the 18th year). Reformed commentator Ligonier suggests the Kings author "placed the material out of chronological order for a theological purpose." [https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/josiahs-covenant-faithfulness](https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/josiahs-covenant-faithfulness)

**Nature of the "Book of the Law":** Most scholars (Constable) identify it as Deuteronomy. Clarke thought it might be Moses' autograph. Selman warns against assuming this supports a late-Deuteronomic-composition theory. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-chronicles-34.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-chronicles-34.html) ; [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-34/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-34/)

**Josiah's death and the "peace" promise:** Views range from "died before the exile" (Guzik/Selman) to "the promise was conditional on obedience; Josiah violated it at Megiddo" (McConville, via Constable). [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-chronicles-34.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-chronicles-34.html)

**Nature of the people's obedience (v. 33):** Guzik emphasizes the positive — "God's Spirit extended the work beyond the king." Gill and Matthew Henry note it was outward compliance masking inner declension, pointing to Jeremiah and Zephaniah as evidence. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-34/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-34/) ; [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_chronicles/34.htm](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_chronicles/34.htm)

## What Could Not Be Found

Due to search/fetch limits, I was unable to retrieve full content for: Ellicott's Commentary verse-by-verse detail, the Pulpit Commentary/Homiletics treatment, Matthew Henry's full verse notes, Spurgeon's full sermon text, the NET Bible translation notes, Catholic/Orthodox commentaries (newadvent.org, catholic.com, oca.org), Lutheran (lcms.org, 1517.org), Methodist/Wesleyan (seedbed.com, wesley.nnu.edu), Pentecostal denominational sites (ag.org, pneumareview.com), and modern scholarship pages (bibleodyssey.org, netbible.org). These would be needed for a fully comprehensive treatment covering all requested traditions.
